question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.
Elucidate
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Explicate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Elucidate" means to make something clear or easy to understand by explaining it in detail. (स्पष्ट करना)
◦ Example: The teacher elucidated the difficult concept with several examples.

• "Explicate" carries the same meaning — to analyse and explain something in detail, making its meaning clear. (विस्तार से स्पष्ट करना)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Exhaust" (थका देना): To use up completely or to tire someone out; unrelated to explaining.

• Option 2: "Examine" (जांचना): To inspect or study something closely, but this does not mean "to explain clearly".

• Option 3: "Oracular" (रहस्यमय/भविष्यवाणी जैसा): Mysterious, ambiguous, or prophetic in the manner of an oracle — nearly opposite to "elucidate", which means to make clear.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "elucidate": clarify, explain, illuminate, expound.

• Do not confuse "elucidate" with "obfuscate" (to make unclear/confuse), which is its near-opposite.

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.
A beast of burden
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. An animal that carries luggage.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "A beast of burden" means an animal (such as a donkey, mule, ox, or horse) that is used to carry heavy loads or luggage. (बोझ ढोने वाला जानवर)
◦ Example: In the mountains, mules are often used as beasts of burden to carry supplies.

• By extension, the phrase can also refer to a person who is overworked and treated like such an animal, but the literal/primary meaning tested here is "an animal that carries loads".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "A liability" (देनदारी/बोझ): Means a debt or a disadvantage — this is not what the idiom denotes.

• Option 3: "A person who works hardly": Confuses "beast of burden" with a hardworking person; besides, "works hardly" itself is grammatically odd (it would mean "barely works").

• Option 4: "A violent man": Unrelated to the idea of carrying burdens.

NOTE

• Other animal-related idioms common in SSC exams: "A wolf in sheep's clothing" (a dangerous person pretending to be harmless), "Let the cat out of the bag" (to reveal a secret), "A bull in a china shop" (a clumsy person).

question:
Select the correct passive form of the given sentence.
The police have apprehended the criminal.
option_1: The criminal had been apprehended by the police.
option_2: The criminal had been apprehend by the police.
option_3: The criminal was apprehended by the police.
option_4: The criminal has been apprehended by the police.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The criminal has been apprehended by the police.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence "The police have apprehended the criminal" is in the Present Perfect Tense, active voice.

• Rule — Present Perfect Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + has/have + V3 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + has/have + been + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "the criminal" becomes the subject (singular, so the auxiliary is "has"); the verb "apprehended" (V3) is retained; and "the police" becomes the agent with "by".
◦ Passive: The criminal has been apprehended by the police.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "had been apprehended" is the passive of the Past Perfect Tense, not the Present Perfect.

• Option 2 is incorrect for the same tense error as Option 1, and additionally uses the wrong past participle "apprehend" instead of "apprehended".

• Option 3 is incorrect because "was apprehended" is the passive of the Simple Past Tense.

NOTE

• "Police" is always treated as a plural noun in English (e.g., "The police are investigating"), but once it becomes the agent in the passive voice, the auxiliary depends on the new subject (here, "the criminal", which is singular), not on "police".

• Common irregular past participles tested in SSC passive-voice questions: catch–caught, apprehend–apprehended, seize–seized, arrest–arrested.

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
Approaching her
P. upon the impacts of county lines drug-running networks
Q. 80th birthday in February next year, Hill's
R. relevance and urgency this time focusing
S. writing has lost none of its immediate
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. QSRP.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence begins with the fixed opening phrase "Approaching her", so the part that logically completes this phrase must come first among P/Q/R/S.

• Q ("80th birthday in February next year, Hill's") logically follows "Approaching her", since it names what is being approached (her 80th birthday) and introduces the subject "Hill's" (writing).

• S ("writing has lost none of its immediate") must follow Q, completing the subject "Hill's writing" with its verb "has lost none of its immediate...".

• R ("relevance and urgency this time focusing") follows S, completing the phrase "immediate relevance and urgency", and introduces "this time focusing...".

• P ("upon the impacts of county lines drug-running networks") logically completes R's "focusing" with its object "upon the impacts...".
◦ Full sentence: "Approaching her 80th birthday in February next year, Hill's writing has lost none of its immediate relevance and urgency this time focusing upon the impacts of county lines drug-running networks."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1 (QSRP).

Additional Information

• Option 2 (SQRP) wrongly places S before Q, breaking the link between "Approaching her" and "80th birthday".

• Option 3 (RPQS) and Option 4 (PQSR) both begin with parts (R or P) that cannot logically follow "Approaching her" and destroy the sentence's meaning.

NOTE

• In parajumble/rearrangement questions, always look for a fixed starting phrase and identify which segment grammatically and logically completes it — this is usually the fastest way to eliminate wrong options.

• Watch for linking words (pronouns, possessives like "her", "its", participles like "focusing") that tie one segment to the next.

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Her failure in life is too much painful for me.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. is too much.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "Her failure in life is too much painful for me" contains an error in the segment "is too much".

• Rule: The word "too" is directly followed by an adjective (too + adjective) to mean "excessively"; "much" should NOT be inserted between "too" and the adjective it modifies (e.g., "too painful", not "too much painful").
◦ Correct: Her failure in life is too painful for me.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "No error" is incorrect because the sentence does contain a genuine error, as explained above.

• Option 2: "painful for me." is grammatically correct on its own and is not the erroneous part.

• Option 4: "Her failure in life" is a correctly formed subject phrase and contains no error.

NOTE

• "Too much" is correctly used before an uncountable noun (e.g., "too much noise", "too much sugar"), not before an adjective.

• Similarly, "too many" is used before plural countable nouns (e.g., "too many mistakes").

• Commonly tested pattern: "too + adjective + to + verb" (e.g., "too painful to bear").

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.
To lose one's head
option_4: To lose the track of time
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. To lose one's self-control.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "To lose one's head" means to panic, become extremely angry, or lose one's self-control, especially in a difficult or stressful situation. (आपा खो देना/नियंत्रण खो देना)
◦ Example: Even in the emergency, the pilot did not lose his head and landed the plane safely.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "To reach nowhere" (कहीं न पहुंचना): Means to make no progress; unrelated to losing composure.

• Option 3: "To have bad memory" (कमजोर याददाश्त होना): This describes forgetfulness, which is a different idiom ("to have a memory like a sieve").

• Option 4: "To lose the track of time" (समय का ध्यान न रहना): Means to become so absorbed in something that one forgets how much time has passed — a different meaning altogether.

NOTE

• Contrast with "To keep one's head", which means the opposite — to remain calm under pressure.

• Related idioms: "To fly off the handle" (to lose temper suddenly), "To hit the roof" (to become very angry), "To keep one's cool" (to stay calm).

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
P. we found that thyroid hormones regulate white bar formation
Q. sea anemone species in which the young fish is recruited
R. and that a shift in hormone levels, associated with ecological
S. differences, results in divergent colour patterns in different
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. PRSQ.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• P ("we found that thyroid hormones regulate white bar formation") is the natural opening, stating the researchers' main finding.

• R ("and that a shift in hormone levels, associated with ecological") follows P with the connector "and that", adding a second finding parallel to the first ("we found that... and that...").

• S ("differences, results in divergent colour patterns in different") continues R's clause, completing "associated with ecological differences" and introducing "results in divergent colour patterns in different...".

• Q ("sea anemone species in which the young fish is recruited") completes S's "different..." with the noun phrase "sea anemone species...".
◦ Full sentence: "...we found that thyroid hormones regulate white bar formation and that a shift in hormone levels, associated with ecological differences, results in divergent colour patterns in different sea anemone species in which the young fish is recruited."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3 (PRSQ).

Additional Information

• Option 1 (SQPR), Option 2 (RSQP) and Option 4 (PQRS) all break the "we found that... and that..." parallel structure or place "different" away from "sea anemone species", producing an incoherent sentence.

NOTE

• The correlative structure "found that X and that Y" is a strong clue in scientific-style rearrangement passages — always look for such parallel connectors to lock segments together.

• Adjectives like "different" must be placed immediately before the noun they qualify (here, "sea anemone species").

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose 'No improvement' as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.
I can sees the mountains in the distance.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. can see.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The given sentence is "I can sees the mountains in the distance."

• Rule — Modal verbs: A modal auxiliary (can, could, may, might, will, would, shall, should, must) is always followed by the base form (V1) of the main verb, never by an -s, -ed, or -ing form.
◦ Correct: I can see the mountains in the distance.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "No improvement" is incorrect because "can sees" is grammatically wrong.

• Option 2: "can seen" is incorrect because "seen" is the past participle (V3), not the base form.

• Option 3: "can saw" is incorrect because "saw" is the simple past form (V2), not the base form.

NOTE

• This rule applies to all modal verbs: e.g., "She can play" (not "can plays"), "He must go" (not "must goes").

• The only modal-like expressions that behave slightly differently are "ought to" and "used to", which are followed by "to + V1".

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose 'No improvement' as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.
The early morning flight is the lest expensive.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. least expensive.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined word in the sentence "The early morning flight is the lest expensive" is misspelled; the correct spelling is "least", the superlative degree of "little", used here in the phrase "the least expensive" (meaning "cheapest").

• Rule: For most two-or-more-syllable adjectives, the superlative degree is formed with "the most/the least" rather than adding "-est" (e.g., least expensive, most beautiful).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "least's expensive" wrongly inserts an apostrophe-s after "least", which is not a possessive noun.

• Option 3: "lastly expensive" incorrectly uses the adverb "lastly" (meaning "finally"), which does not fit the intended comparative sense at all.

• Option 4: "No improvement" is incorrect because "lest" is a spelling error for "least" and must be corrected.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "lest" (a conjunction meaning "in order that... not", e.g., "Speak softly lest you wake the baby") with "least" (superlative of "little").

• Degrees of comparison: little – less – least; much/many – more – most.

question:
Select the correct indirect form of the given sentence.
She said to her maid, "Clean the utensils properly."
option_1: She ordered her maid to clean the utensils properly.
option_2: She commanded her maid that kindly clean the utensils properly.
option_3: She orders her maid to clean the utensils properly.
option_4: She commands her maid that clean the utensils properly.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. She ordered her maid to clean the utensils properly.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The direct sentence "She said to her maid, 'Clean the utensils properly.'" is an imperative sentence (a command) in direct speech.

• Rule — Reporting Imperative Sentences: "Said to" is changed to a verb of command/request such as "ordered", "commanded", "told", "requested" (chosen according to tone) followed by the object and "to" + base verb (V1) of the imperative. Inverted commas and the punctuation of direct speech are removed.
◦ Reported form: Subject + ordered/told + object + to + V1 + rest of sentence.

• Applying the rule: "Clean the utensils properly" (a command) becomes "to clean the utensils properly", and "said to her maid" becomes "ordered her maid".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "She commanded her maid that kindly clean the utensils properly." is incorrect because it wrongly retains the conjunction "that" along with the infinitive structure — imperative reported speech does not use "that + clean" (a finite verb after "that" is ungrammatical here).

• Option 3: "She orders her maid to clean the utensils properly." is incorrect because it keeps the reporting verb in the present tense ("orders") when the reporting verb "said" is in the past tense, requiring "ordered".

• Option 4: "She commands her maid that clean the utensils properly." is incorrect for the same reasons as Options 2 and 3 combined — wrong tense of the reporting verb and an incorrect "that + base verb" structure.

NOTE

• Common reporting verbs for imperative sentences: order/command (for a command), request (for "please" statements, e.g., "requested...to kindly..."), advise (for advice), forbid (for negative commands, e.g., "told...not to").

• A polite request with "please" is reported using "requested" + object + "to", e.g., "Please help me" → "She requested him to help her."

question: Choose the incorrectly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Fantsy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Fantasy" (not "Fantsy") — an imaginative or fanciful mental image, typically one on which desires are based.

• Spelling key: FAN + TA + SY. The word retains the vowel "a" between "t" and "s" (fan-ta-sy); dropping it, as in "Fantsy", is incorrect.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Bubble" is spelled correctly.

• Option 3: "Stormy" is spelled correctly.

• Option 4: "Mince" is spelled correctly.

NOTE

• Related words with the same "-tasy" pattern to watch for: ecstasy, apostasy.

• Commonly misspelt words tested by SSC in similar sets: "definately" (definitely), "recieve" (receive), "occassion" (occasion), "priviledge" (privilege).

question: Choose the sentence with no spelling error.
option_1: I thought I was going to die.
option_2: I thought I was going to diye.
option_3: I thought I was goinng to die.
option_4: I thught I was going to die.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. I thought I was going to die.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Option 1 — "I thought I was going to die." — contains no spelling errors; every word ("thought", "was", "going", "die") is spelled correctly.

• The other three options each contain one misspelled word, as detailed below.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "I thought I was going to diye." is incorrect because "diye" is a misspelling of "die".

• Option 3: "I thought I was goinng to die." is incorrect because "goinng" is a misspelling of "going" (extra "n").

• Option 4: "I thught I was going to die." is incorrect because "thught" is a misspelling of "thought" (missing "o").

NOTE

• A useful strategy for "choose the sentence with no spelling error" questions is to check each option word by word against the others, since usually only one word differs across the four options and that is the target of the error.

• Commonly confused word pairs in SSC spelling questions: die/dye, chief/chef, quiet/quite.

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.
Legit
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Illegal.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Legit" (short for "legitimate") means lawful, permitted by law, or genuine. (वैध/कानूनी)

• Its antonym is "Illegal", meaning not authorised or allowed by law. (अवैध/गैरकानूनी)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Bona fide" (वास्तविक/सच्चा): Means genuine or made in good faith — a synonym of "legit", not its opposite.

• Option 2: "Endorsed" (समर्थित): Means publicly approved or supported — not opposite in meaning to "legit".

• Option 4: "Canonical" (मानक/प्रामाणिक): Means conforming to accepted standards or rules — again close in sense to "legitimate", not its opposite.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "legit/legitimate": lawful, valid, authentic, genuine, rightful.

• Other antonyms often tested alongside: illicit, unlawful, counterfeit, fraudulent.

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.
One who adapts oneself readily to various situations
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Versatile.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Versatile" means a person who adapts easily to many different situations, or someone with a wide range of skills/abilities. (बहुमुखी प्रतिभा वाला)
◦ Example: A versatile actor can play comic, tragic, and villainous roles with equal ease.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Orthodox" (रूढ़िवादी): Means following traditional or established beliefs/practices — almost opposite to being adaptable.

• Option 3: "Fastidious" (नुक्ताचीनी करने वाला): Means excessively particular about details or hard to please; unrelated to adaptability.

• Option 4: "Ardent" (उत्साही/उत्कट): Means passionate or enthusiastic; does not mean adaptable to situations.

NOTE

• Other frequently asked one-word substitutions for personal qualities: "Amateur" (one who pursues something as a hobby, not professionally), "Philanthropist" (one who does charitable work), "Pragmatic" (one who deals with things sensibly and practically).

question:
Select the word that is opposite in meaning (ANTONYM) to the word given below.
Cynical
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Credulous.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Cynical" means distrustful of people's sincerity or motives; believing that people are generally selfish. (संशयवादी/लोगों पर अविश्वास करने वाला)

• Its antonym is "Credulous", meaning too ready to believe things; trusting or gullible. (भोलाभाला/जल्दी विश्वास कर लेने वाला)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Scoffing" (उपहास करने वाला): Means mocking or expressing scorn — close in spirit to cynicism, not its opposite.

• Option 2: "Incredulous" (अविश्वासी): Means unwilling or unable to believe something — this is actually close in meaning to "cynical" (distrustful), not its opposite.

• Option 4: "Sceptical" (संशयवादी): Is a near-synonym of "cynical" (doubting, questioning), not its antonym.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "credulous" (gullible, trusting) with "incredulous" (unbelieving/doubtful) — they are near-opposites of each other despite looking similar.

• Related word: "credible" (believable) — different again from both "credulous" and "incredulous".

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Bacteria are single-celled organisms that can reproduce on its own.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. reproduce on its own.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "Bacteria are single-celled organisms that can reproduce on its own" contains an error in the segment "reproduce on its own".

• Rule: "Bacteria" is a plural noun (the singular form is "bacterium") and is used with the plural verb "are" in this sentence; therefore, the possessive pronoun referring back to it must also be plural — "their", not "its".
◦ Correct: Bacteria are single-celled organisms that can reproduce on their own.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "organisms that can" is grammatically correct and not the source of the error.

• Option 2: "No error" is incorrect because the sentence does contain the pronoun-agreement error described above.

• Option 3: "Bacteria are single-celled" is correct as written; "Bacteria" correctly takes the plural verb "are".

NOTE

• "Bacteria" (plural)/"bacterium" (singular) is a classic Latin-origin plural often tested for subject-verb and pronoun agreement in SSC exams.

• Similar Latin/Greek plurals to remember: criteria/criterion, phenomena/phenomenon, data/datum, media/medium.

question:
Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to the given word.
Chastise
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Extol.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Chastise" means to rebuke or reprimand severely; to punish, especially by beating. (कड़ी डांट लगाना/दंड देना)

• Its antonym is "Extol", meaning to praise enthusiastically; to speak very highly of. (प्रशंसा करना)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Mulct" (जुर्माना लगाना/धोखा देना): Means to extract money from someone by a fine or by deception — a form of punishment, close in spirit to "chastise", not its opposite.

• Option 2: "Keelhaul" (कठोर दंड देना): Means to punish someone severely (originally a naval punishment of dragging a person under a ship's keel) — a near-synonym of "chastise".

• Option 3: "Berate" (डांटना): Means to scold angrily — a direct synonym of "chastise", not its antonym.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "chastise": reprimand, rebuke, admonish, castigate.

• Other words meaning "to praise" often tested as its antonym: commend, applaud, laud, eulogize.

question:
Given below are four jumbled sentences. Pick the option that gives their correct order.
P. To stop Caesar from gaining too much power, Brutus and the conspirators kill him on the Ides of March.
Q. Brutus and his friend Cassius lose and kill themselves, leaving Antony to rule in Rome.
R. Mark Antony drives the conspirators out of Rome and fights them in a battle.
S. The tale of Julius Caesar involves jealous conspirators who convince Caesar's most trusted ally Brutus to join their assassination plot against Caesar.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. SPRQ.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• S ("The tale of Julius Caesar involves jealous conspirators who convince Caesar's most trusted ally Brutus to join their assassination plot against Caesar.") is the natural opening, introducing the story and its central characters.

• P ("To stop Caesar from gaining too much power, Brutus and the conspirators kill him on the Ides of March.") logically follows S, describing the assassination plot (introduced in S) being carried out.

• R ("Mark Antony drives the conspirators out of Rome and fights them in a battle.") follows P chronologically — after the assassination, Antony retaliates against the conspirators.

• Q ("Brutus and his friend Cassius lose and kill themselves, leaving Antony to rule in Rome.") logically concludes the sequence — as a result of losing the battle described in R, Brutus and Cassius die and Antony ends up ruling Rome.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2 (SPRQ).

Additional Information

• Option 1 (SQPR), Option 3 (QPSR) and Option 4 (SQRP) all disturb this cause-and-effect chronology — for instance, placing Q (the deaths and Antony's rule) before P (the assassination) or R (the battle) makes the sequence of events logically impossible.

NOTE

• In narrative/story-based rearrangement passages, identify the chronological/causal order of events (introduction → action → consequence → resolution) rather than relying only on grammatical linking words.

• Look for a sentence that names/introduces the subject (here, "The tale of Julius Caesar...") as a strong candidate for the opening sentence.

question:
Select the most appropriate 'one word' for the expression given below.
A place where public records are preserved.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Archive.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Archive" means a place or collection in which public records, historical documents, or other important materials are kept and preserved. (अभिलेखागार)
◦ Example: The old manuscripts were carefully preserved in the national archive.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "Library" (पुस्तकालय): A place where books are kept for reading or borrowing — not specifically for official/public records.

• Option 3: "Court Room" (न्यायालय कक्ष): A room where legal proceedings are held; not a storage place for records in general.

• Option 4: "Diary" (डायरी): A personal notebook for daily entries; unrelated to the preservation of public records.

NOTE

• Other commonly tested "place" one-word substitutions: "Museum" (a place where objects of historical/artistic/scientific interest are kept), "Sanctuary" (a place of safety/refuge for animals), "Asylum" (a place of refuge/shelter, or an institution for the mentally ill).

question:
Select the most appropriate 'one word' for the expression given below.
Something that is no longer in use.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Obsolete.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Obsolete" means something that is no longer in use, produced, or needed; out of date. (अप्रचलित/चलन से बाहर)
◦ Example: Typewriters have become obsolete with the advent of computers.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Absolute" (पूर्ण/निरपेक्ष): Means complete or not qualified/diminished in any way — unrelated to being out of use.

• Option 2: "Vogue" (प्रचलन/फैशन): Means the prevailing fashion or the state of being popular — the near opposite of "no longer in use".

• Option 4: "Contemporary" (समकालीन): Means belonging to the present time or existing at the same time as something/someone else — again nearly opposite to "obsolete".

NOTE

• "Obsolete" is often confused with "obsolescent" (becoming obsolete/going out of use, i.e. in the process rather than already out of use).

• Related one-word substitution: "Archaic" (very old or old-fashioned, especially of language).

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

Sudden changes in the gilts market are (1)______, but when they do happen it can cause (2)________ problems for certain types of pension scheme, as UK pension savers (3)________ recently. In addition to raising borrowing costs for the government, the market mayhem following September's mini-budget (4)______ many pension providers to quickly cash in some of their holdings to try to weather the (5)_____.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. rare.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "Sudden changes in the gilts market are rare, but when they do happen it can cause..." — the word "but" signals a contrast: the changes are rare (uncommon), yet still capable of causing problems when they do occur.

• Rule — Cloze context clues: The contrasting conjunction "but" indicates that the missing word must express an idea that sets up a contrast with "can cause problems" — i.e., that such changes do not happen often.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "easy" does not fit — the sentence is about how often changes happen, not how easy they are.

• Option 3: "severe" would create a contradictory sentence — if changes were already described as "severe", the following clause "but when they do happen it can cause..." would be redundant, since "severe" already implies a harmful impact.

• Option 4: "high" does not fit the sense of "how often" the changes occur, and is not the natural collocation used to describe the frequency of market changes here.

NOTE

• In fill-in-the-blank/cloze passages, always look for connecting/contrasting words ("but", "however", "although", "yet") immediately before or after the blank — they are the strongest clue to the required meaning.

• Synonyms of "rare" often tested: infrequent, uncommon, scarce, occasional.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 3: "scanty" means insufficient/meagre — the opposite of the serious tone the passage conveys about the impact of sudden market changes.

• Option 4: "bulky" means large in size/mass, a word typically used for physical objects, not for abstract "problems".

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage some of the words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the correct answer for the given blank out of the four alternatives.

Sudden changes in the gilts market are (1)______, but when they do happen it can cause (2)________ problems for certain types of pension scheme, as UK pension savers (3)________ recently. In addition to raising borrowing costs for the government, the market mayhem following September's mini-budget (4)______ many pension providers to quickly cash in some of their holdings to try to weather the (5)_____.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. have seen.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "...as UK pension savers have seen recently." The subject "UK pension savers" is plural, and the time marker "recently" points to an action that started in the past and connects to the present — this is the hallmark of the Present Perfect Tense.

• Rule — Present Perfect Tense: Subject (plural) + have + V3 (past participle), used for actions completed at an indefinite time before now, especially when linked to the present situation with words like "recently", "already", "just", "yet".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "seen" is incorrect on its own, as it is only the past participle and needs an auxiliary verb ("have"/"has") to form a complete, grammatically correct verb phrase.

• Option 3: "has seen" is incorrect because the subject "UK pension savers" is plural, requiring the plural auxiliary "have", not the singular "has".

• Option 4: "did saw" is incorrect because it wrongly combines the past auxiliary "did" with the past-tense form "saw"; after "did", only the base form ("see") can be used, and even then, the Simple Past would not carry the "recently...connected to present result" sense as well as the Present Perfect does.

NOTE

• Present Perfect is frequently signalled in cloze passages by time expressions such as "recently", "already", "so far", "up to now", "just".

• Remember the subject-verb agreement rule for auxiliaries: plural subject → have; singular subject (he/she/it) → has.

solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. forced.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "...the market mayhem following September's mini-budget forced many pension providers to quickly cash in some of their holdings..." — "forced...to" is the natural collocation meaning compelled or obliged (someone) to do something, matching the urgency implied by "mayhem" and "quickly cash in".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "uncontrived" means natural/genuine (not artificial), which does not fit the sense of compelling providers to act.

• Option 3: "seized" would normally need a direct object (e.g., "seized the opportunity") rather than the "...to + verb" pattern used here, so it does not fit the sentence's grammar or sense as well as "forced" does.

• Option 4: "slated" means scheduled/criticised, neither of which fits the meaning of compelling pension providers to sell holdings.

NOTE

• The collocation "force/oblige/compel someone to do something" is a common pattern tested in SSC cloze/error-spotting questions.

• Distinguish "forced" (compelled) from "enforced" (to compel observance of a law/rule) — a commonly confused pair.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "pond" similarly does not fit; "weather the pond" is not an established expression.
